passage:
"Sarita, can you water the tulsi and fold the towels before dinner?"
"Yes, Mummy! Of course!"
An hour later: "Sarita, the towels?"
"Oh! I forgot. Sorry! I'll do it right now!"
Half an hour later Himani-didi came in. "Mummy, the towels are still in the basket. And the tulsi's dry again."
"Sarita?"
"I totally forgot! My brain is so bad."
"That's the fifth time this week, beta."
Sarita looked at her toes. Didi sat down next to her. "You know what I think? I think you hate folding towels."
"...I do hate folding towels. They're so boring. And Didi only has to do the dishes."
"Then say that," Mummy said. "We can talk about swapping. But saying yes and then forgetting isn't fair on anyone."

qa.q: What two jobs did Mummy ask Sarita to do?
qa.a: Water the tulsi and fold the towels.

qa.q: Why did Sarita keep saying yes and then forgetting?
qa.a: Sarita felt resentful about the boring job, which seemed unfair next to Didi's dishes, but found it hard to say no directly, so the resistance came out as forgetting.

qa.q: Which choice in the conversation opened a better way forward?
qa.a: Didi naming the likely feeling, then Mummy inviting Sarita to say it and offering to talk about swapping. 🙂

qa.q: How might Himani-didi feel about the dry tulsi and the unfolded towels?
qa.a: Probably irritated at noticing the undone jobs again, and perhaps a little defensive when the dishes were brought up.

grounding: A child cheerfully agrees to a chore and keeps forgetting, until Mummy and Didi help Sarita say directly what the problem is.

passage:
Last month Rafiq Chacha from next door asked if I'd feed his parrots every evening while his leg was in plaster. I said, "Yes, yes, definitely!" And then, three evenings out of five, I "forgot". Mummy had to go instead, and she looked at me funny at dinner.
The truth, which I didn't even tell myself then, was that the parrots scare me. They screech and bite the bars when you open the cage. But Chacha is so kind, always giving me toffees, that saying no felt rude.
Last week Mummy asked why I kept agreeing. I cried a bit and told her. Then I told Chacha. He laughed and said, "Arre, just say so!" Now I water his plants instead. I'm Jahnavi, and plants don't bite.

qa.q: What did Rafiq Chacha ask Jahnavi to do?
qa.a: Feed his parrots every evening while his leg was in plaster.

qa.q: Why did Jahnavi keep 'forgetting' instead of saying no?
qa.a: Jahnavi was scared of the parrots but felt that saying no to kind Chacha would be rude, so the resistance came out sideways as forgetting.

qa.q: What turning point let Jahnavi stop forgetting?
qa.a: Telling Mummy the truth when she asked, then telling Chacha, which led to a new job Jahnavi could really do.

qa.q: How might Mummy have felt going to feed the parrots herself?
qa.a: Probably puzzled and a bit annoyed, sensing something was off, which is why she later asked Jahnavi why she kept agreeing.

grounding: A child who couldn't say no to a kind neighbour agreed to a frightening job and kept 'forgetting' it, until the truth came out.

passage:
Class 4 teacher's note, Friday
For three weeks Shreya has been on the rota to wipe the board and water the class plants. Each morning she agrees brightly, "Yes, Nazia Ma'am!", and each afternoon the board is still full and the plants are dry. When I remind her, she says, "Oh no, I totally forgot!" with a big smile.
Today I asked her quietly, "Is there a job on the rota you'd rather not do?" After a pause she said, "The chalk dust makes me sneeze, and the boys at the back laugh when I sneeze."
We've swapped her to handing out notebooks. I also told her she can always tell me no, or ask to swap, and I won't be cross.

qa.q: Which two jobs was Shreya on the rota for?
qa.a: Wiping the board and watering the class plants.

qa.q: Why might Shreya say 'I totally forgot!' with a big smile?
qa.a: She didn't want the board job because of the sneezing and the laughter, but felt she couldn't say no, so a cheerful 'forgot' was easier.

qa.q: Which choice of the teacher's worked, and why?
qa.a: Asking quietly whether there was a job Shreya would rather not do, and promising she could say no or swap, which made a direct refusal safe.

qa.q: What would change for Shreya now that Nazia Ma'am has said 'I won't be cross'?
qa.a: She may feel safe to say no openly next time, so she won't need to 'forget' to show she doesn't want a job.

grounding: A teacher notices a girl who agrees brightly to class jobs and then forgets them, and makes it safe for her to say no directly.

passage:
Dear Diary,
Today Ammi asked again if I'd go up and help Maria with her reading at six. I said, "Yes, Ammi, of course!" in my best voice. Then at six I suddenly had to sort my stickers. And have a long bath. By the time I came out it was seven, and Maria's mother had gone back upstairs.
That's the fourth time this week. Ammi thinks I'm just forgetful.
Truth is, I don't want to. Maria is six and she cries when she gets a word wrong, and it takes up all my cartoon time. But when Ammi asks, her face is so hopeful that "no" gets stuck. So "yes" comes out, and then my feet just go somewhere else.
Maybe tomorrow I'll forget again.
Dilnaz

qa.q: What did Dilnaz do at six instead of helping Maria?
qa.a: Sorted stickers and had a long bath.

qa.q: Why does "no" get stuck for Dilnaz?
qa.a: Ammi's face looks so hopeful that refusing feels impossible, so Dilnaz agrees cheerfully and then resists by "forgetting".

qa.q: What could Dilnaz try instead of forgetting again?
qa.a: Telling Ammi honestly that the sessions are hard and take all the cartoon time, and maybe offering two evenings a week instead of every day.

qa.q: What might Maria's mother think after going back upstairs four times?
qa.a: She may feel let down and puzzled, thinking Dilnaz is unreliable, without knowing Dilnaz never really wanted to say yes.

grounding: Shows a child who cheerfully agrees to an unwanted job and then keeps forgetting, because saying no directly feels impossible.

passage:
In their village near Thrissur, Umma and Elizabeth aunty from next door ran a small tea shop by the bus stop. Every afternoon Umma asked, "Salma, wash the glasses after school, okay?" and Salma, nine, said, "Yes, Umma! Of course!" with a big smile.
Every afternoon she then forgot. She went to see the ducks on the canal, or started a very long game of hopscotch. When she came back, the glasses were already shining on the rack.
On Friday Elizabeth aunty caught her arm, gently. "Salma, you say yes every day. And every day you disappear. Is there something about the glasses?"
Salma twisted her plait. "The soap smells horrible. It stays on my hands all evening. But Umma is so tired, I can't say no."
Elizabeth aunty laughed softly. "Then say that. We'll find you another job."

qa.q: Where did Salma go instead of washing the glasses?
qa.a: To see the ducks on the canal, or to start a very long game of hopscotch.

qa.q: Why did Salma keep saying "Yes, Umma!" if she didn't want to wash the glasses?
qa.a: Umma looked so tired that saying no felt wrong, so Salma agreed cheerfully and then resisted by disappearing instead.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth aunty's question make possible?
qa.a: It gave Salma a safe chance to say the real reason, the soap smell, so the job can be swapped instead of the forgetting going on 🙂

qa.q: How might Umma see the shining glasses on the rack each day?
qa.a: Umma may think Salma simply forgets, and perhaps feel tired or let down, not knowing Salma hates the soap but can't say so.

grounding: Illustrates a child who says yes brightly to a chore and then always slips away, her resistance coming out sideways because a direct no feels impossible.
